questions.prompt: Which statement best describes the OS from the system perspective?
options: It translates every high-level programming language into machine code.
It allocates and controls hardware resources shared by programs.
It is only the graphical desktop that users can see.
It replaces the CPU instruction set with a programming language.
questions.explanation: The OS manages resources such as CPU time, memory and devices and controls their use. A desktop interface is one way to interact with this wider system.
questions.misconception: Do not define the entire OS solely by one interface or utility.

refs.locator: OS job: User view and System view

questions.prompt: In the basic von Neumann model, which resource is shared by instructions and data?
options: The same main memory/address space and communication path.
One separate instruction memory and one separate data memory.
A dedicated interrupt handler for each arithmetic operation.
Only the keyboard input buffer.
questions.explanation: The basic von Neumann organization stores instructions and data in a common memory system. Separate instruction and data paths are characteristic of the basic Harvard model. Real machines may combine design ideas.
questions.misconception: A split L1 instruction/data cache alone does not mean the entire computer uses a pure Harvard memory model.

refs.locator: Slides 36–39: Instruction cycle and von Neumann architecture

questions.prompt: What happens in the decode stage of the simplified fetch–decode–execute cycle?
options: The OS always switches to another process.
The result is automatically written to a disk.
The CPU determines the operation and operands specified by the instruction.
The firmware reloads the kernel.
questions.explanation: Fetch retrieves an instruction; decode interprets its encoded operation; execute performs the required operation. Data transfer or result storage depends on the instruction.
questions.misconception: Fetching an instruction and interpreting it are different steps.

questions.prompt: Which operation, as phrased, requires privileged kernel handling in the course model?
options: Adding two ordinary integers already held in an application’s registers.
Formatting a string inside an application buffer.
Choosing a word’s font in an already running editor.
Handling a device’s hardware interrupt in its ISR.
questions.explanation: The interrupt handler runs with the privileges needed to handle the hardware event. Ordinary computations can execute in user mode; related I/O may separately require kernel services.
questions.misconception: A user-facing activity can contain user-mode work and separate kernel operations. Classify the specified operation.

refs.locator: Exercise 2-3: User Mode or Kernel Mode

questions.prompt: A process calls an OS service; later a device signals completion. Which distinction is correct?
options: The call is synchronous with the calling instruction; device completion is asynchronous to the interrupted instruction stream.
Both events are necessarily generated by the same instruction.
The hardware interrupt is selected by the system-call number.
The system call is always an error and the interrupt is always a successful operation.
questions.explanation: The request originates from the executing program; the device can notify the CPU independently of that program’s current instruction. The system-call interface and interrupt-vector mechanism serve different roles.
questions.misconception: A system-call table and an interrupt-vector table are not interchangeable.

questions.prompt: Use the course convention: base = 6000 and limit = 800 bytes, with limit meaning the region length. Which physical address is the highest valid one?
questions.explanation: The valid interval is base ≤ address < base + limit: 6000 through 6799 inclusive. Address 6800 is the first byte beyond the allowed 800-byte region.
questions.misconception: Do not include base + limit when limit is a size. This question states the convention explicitly.

questions.prompt: A process in the five-state teaching model completes the I/O event it was waiting for. What is its immediate next state before a CPU is assigned?
options: Terminated
Running
New
Ready
questions.explanation: I/O completion makes the process eligible for CPU service, so it enters Ready. The scheduler/dispatcher must subsequently select it to run.
questions.misconception: Waiting → Running skips the ready/scheduling step in the stated model.

questions.prompt: A process successfully executes an exec-family call. What is the defining effect?
options: A second process is created and both execute the original program.
The current process waits for every process on the computer.
The current process image is replaced by a new program; its PID is retained.
The current process always becomes a zombie immediately.
questions.explanation: exec replaces the calling process’s program image. fork creates a new process. A program often uses fork followed by exec, but those are distinct operations.
questions.misconception: Do not count exec itself as creation of another PID.

questions.prompt: After the OS establishes a shared-memory region, what responsibility remains essential for cooperating processes that update the same data?
options: Coordinate access so that conflicting updates do not race.
Copy every byte through a new system call on every load.
Give both processes the same PID.
Disable all file-system services permanently.
questions.explanation: Shared memory allows direct access to common data, but sharing does not make multi-step updates atomic. Coordination is needed when operations conflict.
questions.misconception: A shared address range is a communication mechanism, not an automatic synchronization solution.

refs.locator: Slides 32–36: IPC models and shared memory

questions.prompt: Which set normally belongs separately to each thread in one process?
options: The executable’s code and all global variables.
The process’s address space and open-file table only.
The physical CPU and its entire cache hierarchy.
Program counter, register state and stack.
questions.explanation: Each thread needs its own execution position, registers and call stack. Threads in a process typically share code, data and resources such as open files.
questions.misconception: Sharing an address space does not make every thread execute with one shared stack.

questions.prompt: Assume 25% of a program is serial, 75% is perfectly parallel, two equal cores are used, and there is no additional overhead. What speedup does Amdahl’s Law predict?
questions.explanation: Speedup = 1 / (0.25 + 0.75/2) = 1/0.625 = 1.6. The serial portion limits the gain even in this ideal model.
questions.misconception: Dividing all the work by two incorrectly parallelizes the serial quarter.

questions.prompt: Three processes arrive at time 0 in queue order P1, P2, P3, with CPU bursts 6, 2 and 4. Under non-preemptive FCFS, with no I/O or switch cost, what is the total waiting time across all three?
options: 12 time units
6 time units
14 time units
18 time units
questions.explanation: P1 starts at 0 and waits 0; P2 starts at 6 and waits 6; P3 starts at 8 and waits 8. The sum is 14. Its average would be 14/3, which was not requested.
questions.misconception: Burst-time sum and waiting-time sum measure different quantities.

questions.prompt: All three processes arrive at time 0: P1 has burst 6, P2 burst 2 and P3 burst 4. Under non-preemptive SJF with no I/O or switch cost, what is the execution order?
questions.explanation: At each dispatch, choose the available process with the shortest burst: 2, then 4, then 6. Equal arrivals and unequal burst lengths remove tie ambiguity.
questions.misconception: SJF chooses among arrived ready work; it does not normally wait for an unknown future job.

questions.prompt: P1 and P2 arrive at 0 in that queue order with bursts 5 and 3. Round Robin uses quantum 2 and zero switch overhead. Define response time as first CPU start minus arrival. What is P2’s response time?
questions.explanation: P1 first runs from 0 to 2, then P2 first starts at 2. P2’s response time is 2 − 0 = 2, regardless of when it finally completes.
questions.misconception: Response time is not completion time or total waiting accumulated over every turn.

questions.prompt: counter starts at 5. Producer reads 5 and computes 6 in a private register. Consumer reads 5 and computes 4. Producer writes 6; consumer then writes 4. What is the final counter value in this specified interleaving?
questions.explanation: The final shared-memory write is the consumer’s stale calculation, 4. A correctly synchronized increment plus decrement should leave 5; this order loses the producer’s update.
questions.misconception: A source-language ++ or -- is not guaranteed to be an indivisible shared update.

questions.prompt: A counting semaphore represents two identical available resources and starts at 2. Two processes each successfully perform one atomic wait operation and hold their resources. With no signal yet, what happens to a third process’s wait?
options: It creates a third resource automatically.
It deletes both current holders.
It cannot acquire a resource until one becomes available.
It must immediately enter the protected operation.
questions.explanation: Both permits are held, so the available-resource count is zero. The third acquisition must wait; whether it spins or sleeps depends on the semaphore implementation.
questions.misconception: A counting semaphore enforces a resource count; it is not a request to manufacture resources.

refs.locator: Slides 38–39: Semaphore wait, signal and resource counts

questions.prompt: A /proc/cpuinfo file that reports size 0 can still return CPU information when read.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Many /proc contents are produced by the kernel at read time, so their reported file size need not describe the readable data.
questions.misconception: A procfs virtual file need not behave like a disk-backed text file.

questions.prompt: Running an ordinary arithmetic instruction as the root user means that instruction necessarily executes in CPU kernel mode.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Root is an account/credential identity. A root user-space program still executes ordinary instructions in user mode and enters the kernel through controlled mechanisms for services.
questions.misconception: User identities and CPU privilege levels are different dimensions.

questions.prompt: Every system call necessarily causes the CPU to switch to a different process.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: The CPU can enter the kernel to service the current process and return to that same process. Blocking or scheduling decisions may cause a switch, but a system call alone does not require one.
questions.misconception: A mode transition is not automatically a process context switch.

refs.locator: Dual Mode Operation and System Call Implementation

questions.prompt: A zombie process has already exited, but its parent has not yet collected the retained exit status.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: The executable work is finished. A small kernel record remains for status collection; the zombie is not a sleeping process that can be resumed with CONT.
questions.misconception: Exited does not always mean all accounting information has already been collected.

questions.prompt: In the classic many-to-one threading model, several user threads mapped to one kernel thread can execute simultaneously on several CPU cores.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Only one kernel-schedulable execution entity exists for those mapped user threads, so they cannot use multiple cores in parallel through that mapping.
questions.misconception: Many user threads do not imply many kernel threads.

questions.prompt: If Round Robin’s quantum is at least as large as every CPU burst in a fixed ready queue, and there are no further arrivals or I/O, its execution order becomes the queue’s FCFS order.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Every process completes its burst on its first turn, so no unfinished process is rotated back to the queue. The explicit assumptions remove later-arrival and I/O complications.
questions.misconception: A larger quantum does not make Round Robin become shortest-job-first.

refs.locator: Round Robin: q large implies FIFO/FCFS

questions.prompt: Mutual exclusion by itself proves that every waiting process will eventually enter its critical section.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Mutual exclusion prevents simultaneous conflicting entry. Progress and bounded waiting are separate requirements concerned with continuing to admit work and limiting postponement.
questions.misconception: Preventing overlap does not automatically prevent starvation.

questions.prompt: A low-priority process may starve while higher-priority processes continue completing useful work.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Starvation is indefinite deprivation of a particular process; the whole system need not stop. A deadlocked set instead cannot advance because its members wait on dependencies within the set.
questions.misconception: Starvation does not require every process to be blocked.

questions.prompt: A video-call application uses the same camera API on two different camera models. Separately, the OS decides which application may use the camera. Which pairing best describes these two roles?
options: Both are only arithmetic operations.
The API hides hardware differences (abstraction); access decisions manage sharing (arbitration).
The API is arbitration; access decisions are only persistence.
Neither role belongs to an OS.
questions.explanation: Abstraction presents a usable interface without requiring device-specific details. Arbitration determines how shared resources are allocated. The same practical service can need both.
questions.misconception: A feature may combine abstraction and arbitration rather than fitting only one label.

questions.prompt: A program initiates a print operation through a kernel service and then the CPU executes other work. Later, the printer controller raises an interrupt. Which explanation is correct?
options: The printer must directly overwrite the application’s code to resume it.
The application chooses the ISR by changing its own PID.
The print system call must have been an asynchronous hardware interrupt.
The controller’s interrupt is a later event; an interrupt handler services it, and execution can resume according to OS scheduling.
questions.explanation: The synchronous service request starts work; the device’s later asynchronous notification invokes interrupt handling. The interrupted process need not be the one that requested printing, and a return can restore the appropriate prior privilege context.
questions.misconception: Do not merge the system-call initiation and later device notification into one identical event.

questions.prompt: A parent has one unfinished child and calls a blocking wait for it. The child later exits. Which description best fits this behavior?
options: The parent waits for the child’s termination and can then obtain its exit status.
The parent’s wait starts another copy of the child program.
The child must become the parent’s thread and share its stack.
The parent must consume CPU continuously until the child exits.
questions.explanation: A blocking wait can suspend the parent while the child runs; on completion, the parent can receive child status. Waiting does not require a busy loop or another child creation.
questions.misconception: Blocking in wait differs from repeatedly polling while occupying CPU time.

questions.prompt: A photo editor assigns four workers separate quarters of the same image, and each worker applies the same blur operation. Which description fits best?
options: Task parallelism because each worker performs an unrelated operation.
No parallelism is possible because the image is one file.
Data parallelism because the same operation runs on separate data subsets.
Kernel-mode execution because the image has four quarters.
questions.explanation: Data parallelism partitions input while applying the same operation. Task parallelism assigns different operations, such as reading, filtering and writing. Correct handling of dependencies at image boundaries is still needed.
questions.misconception: Splitting data among workers does not eliminate every dependency automatically.

refs.locator: Types of parallelism; multicore programming challenges

questions.prompt: P1 arrives at 0 with burst 8. P2 arrives at 1 with burst 3. Under SRT, with no I/O or overhead, what should happen at time 1?
options: P1 must keep running because SRT is non-preemptive.
P1 is preempted because its remaining 7 is longer than P2’s 3.
P2 must wait until time 8 because it arrived later.
Both processes execute simultaneously on the stated single CPU.
questions.explanation: SRT compares remaining work among ready processes. At time 1, P1 has used 1 of 8 units, leaving 7, so the newly arrived three-unit job has the shorter remaining time.
questions.misconception: Do not compare only P1’s original burst or apply FCFS rules to SRT.

questions.prompt: Process A holds a board and waits for a pen held by B. Process B holds the pen and waits for the board held by A. Neither releases its held resource while waiting, and no outside action intervenes. What is this situation?
options: Normal mutual exclusion with guaranteed progress.
Only one process doing slow I/O.
A correct counting-semaphore initialization.
Deadlock: the processes are waiting on each other and cannot proceed.
questions.explanation: Each process holds what the other needs and waits without releasing it. Under the stated assumptions neither can advance. This is stronger than one process simply losing repeated scheduling opportunities.
questions.misconception: Being blocked temporarily is not necessarily deadlock; the circular dependency and no-release assumptions matter.

questions.prompt:
An illustrative lscpu output shows:
Socket(s): 2
Core(s) per socket: 3
Thread(s) per core: 2
For this uniform topology, how many logical CPUs should CPU(s) show?
questions.explanation: 2 sockets × 3 cores per socket × 2 hardware threads per core = 12 logical CPUs. Physical cores total 6.
questions.misconception: Do not stop at the physical-core count when asked for logical CPUs.

questions.prompt: An illustrative free -h line shows free = 0.8 GiB, buff/cache = 4.9 GiB and available = 5.3 GiB. Which conclusion is justified?
options: Some cached memory can be reclaimed, so available can exceed completely unused free memory.
Only 0.8 GiB can ever be used by another application.
The displayed values prove that RAM is broken.
available must always equal free plus all buff/cache exactly.
questions.explanation: available estimates memory usable by new workloads without swapping and can include reclaimable cached pages. It is not simply a promise that every cached byte is reclaimable.
questions.misconception: Do not infer exhaustion from free alone or assume all displayed categories are independent.

refs.locator: Part C: free -h and memory checkpoint

questions.prompt:
A regular file is displayed as:
-rw-r----- 1 student learners ... note.txt
Ignoring ACLs and special privileges, which statement matches its mode bits?
options: Owner can read only; group can read/write; others can execute.
Owner, group and others can all read.
Owner can execute the file because it begins with -.
Owner can read/write; group can read; others have no permission.
questions.explanation: After the file-type character, rw- is owner 6, r-- is group 4 and --- is others 0: mode 640.
questions.misconception: The first - indicates a regular file; it is not an execute permission.

questions.prompt:
In Bash, suppose ls fails with status 2, while cat successfully reads err.txt:
ls /nothing 2> err.txt
cat err.txt
echo $?
What does echo print?
options: 2, because $? permanently remembers the first error.
0, because the most recently completed command was successful cat.
1, because stderr was redirected.
The contents of err.txt, because $? is a filename.
questions.explanation: The successful cat replaces the prior status. To inspect ls, echo $? immediately after ls or first save status=$?. This corrects the ordering error in the manual’s Step 10 example.
questions.misconception: The presence of an error message inside a file does not make cat fail when it reads that file successfully.

questions.prompt:
After kill -STOP "$PID", ps shows:
PID  STAT COMMAND
4821 T    sleep
What is the best interpretation?
options: The process is stopped and still exists with the same PID.
The executable sleep has been deleted from disk.
PID 4821 is necessarily a zombie.
The process is guaranteed to be consuming its entire CPU quantum.
questions.explanation: T is the stopped state. SIGSTOP suspends execution without terminating the process; SIGCONT can resume it.
questions.misconception: A stopped process is neither a sleeping S process nor an exited Z process.

questions.prompt: jobs -l reports "Running sleep 3600 &", while ps reports state S for the same PID. Which explanation is correct?
options: One command must be corrupt because Running and S cannot coexist.
The process has exited but the shell is unaware forever.
The shell job is continuing, while the process is interruptibly sleeping for its timer.
The process is a zombie that is executing CPU instructions.
questions.explanation: The shell’s job status distinguishes running/continuing work from stopped or completed work. Linux S describes a live process currently waiting for an event. The labels answer different questions.
questions.misconception: A shell job marked Running is not guaranteed to have Linux state R.

auditNotes: All 36 questions are independently authored practice, not official GIU exam items or a claim about official exam format, marks or duration.
Distribution: 16 multiple choice, 8 true/false, 6 single-choice scenarios and 6 single-choice Linux-output questions. Each has exactly one indexed correct option.
Scope follows the user clarification to include all six provided lecture PDFs by title, without inventing lecture numbering; Labs 1–3 remain the practical scope.
Every item includes a source-document topic or section. Examples and numerical values are independently prepared unless explicitly described as the course convention.
Scheduling questions state arrivals, tie conditions, CPU count, I/O and overhead assumptions to keep grading objective.
The Lab 2 exit-status sequencing error is corrected: successful cat replaces the earlier ls status. GNU Bash manual supports this correction.
Technical review checks distinguish mode changes from process switches, root credentials from kernel mode, Ready from Running, and shell Running from Linux R.
Objective question results measure performance on this bank, not a probability of passing the exam. No free-text keyword grading is included.
